en: It is naturally so that the flourishing or decline of the Way depends upon the person. When one finds such a person, the Way flourishes;
when such a person perishes, the Way declines. It is said, "The person can broaden the Way, and the Way relies on the person to be broadened. This is precisely what it means.

Is this not what is meant? The Way of our Buddha consists solely of precepts (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Yet, it is the precepts alone that sustain the life-force of the Way.
Thus, Master Nanshan said: "The Vinaya is the life-force of the Dharma; if it is propagated, the life-force is preserved.

If it is not propagated, the True Dharma will perish. Alas! How could the precepts ever be discarded? As for the Vinaya in China, since the time of the Great Wisdom Patriarch Lingzhi entered [the land]...
Following the era of the Soundless Samādhi (Muktsuṇḍa), although there have been individuals who appeared from generation to generation, its dharma gradually faded.

From the Yuan and Ming dynasties onward, the authentic models were entirely lost. During the Wanli period, Master Gulü emerged as a preeminent figure in the world, and the dharma flourished once again.
It is also said that the Way is propagated through people.
The Vinaya Master’s name was Ruxing; his courtesy name was Guxin. He was the son of the Yang family of Liyang.

Having left secular life, he lamented that the study of the Vinaya had fallen into ruin and set out on foot to pay homage at Mount Wutai, seeking an audience with Mañjuśrī to receive the precepts. Upon reaching the middle of the mountains, he saw an old woman holding...
Sengqie asked, "What do you seek? He replied, "I seek to see Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and personally receive the full precepts.
The old woman said, "Have you brought your robe? He replied, "Not yet. The old woman said, "I give this robe to you.
The Master took the robe in his hand. The old woman pointed her finger and said, "Is that not Mañjuśrī? As soon as he looked back, the old woman was gone; the Bodhisattva remained amidst the clouds.
The Master reached down with his hand and touched the head of the monk, saying, "Monk Guxin, Mañjuśrī has finished conferring the precepts upon you.

At these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment into the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground; he regarded the Vinaya of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna as if it had flowed forth from within his own breast.

He subsequently returned to Jinling to restore the monastic precepts. At that time, there was the Dharma Master Xuelang, who had been commissioned by imperial decree to repair the Precious Pagoda at Changgan.
As the work neared completion, the pinnacle of the pagoda proved difficult to hoist. The Master was displeased; after a short while, he leaned on his armrest and fell asleep.

In a dream, a divine being consoled him, saying: "In the future, the Venerable Upāli shall ring his staff as he circumambulates the pagoda, and the pinnacle will drop into its socket of its own accord."
What doubt could there be? At dawn the next day, when the Master led his disciples to circumambulate the stupa while holding their staffs, the reliquary (stūpa) ascended on its own.
All the people of the world believed this to be Upāli turning the wheel of Dharma once again. At that time, Emperor Shenzong composed a eulogy, saying:

"Beholding his countenance, one knows his character. He entered samādhi and severed the six sense-dusts. Upāli of old, the ancient mind of today. He passed away in tranquility; his posthumous title was Huiyun (Wisdom Cloud). His...
The successor to the Dharma was the Vinaya Master Sammai.
The Vinaya Master’s name was Jiguang, and his style name was Sammai. He was the son of the Qian family of Guazhu.

Initially, he relied upon Dharma Master Xuelang to study the teachings and contemplations of the Xianshou school. Subsequently, he sought out Vinaya Master Guxin to receive the full precepts at Ganlin Temple in Runzhou.
At Lushan Temple, he attended [his teacher] for many years, devoting himself solely to the Vinaya precepts. His master, admiring his conduct and understanding, transmitted the *Vinaya* to him.
When the Master first began his travels in Yuzhang, both monastics and laypeople earnestly requested that he confer the full ordination at Donglin Temple on Mount Lu.
Suddenly, eighteen white lotuses with a thousand petals emerged from the dry land. This was reminiscent of when the Great Master Huiyuan was about to pass away...
He addressed the assembly, saying, "If the white lotuses should bloom once more, I shall return to teach and transform you. From the Jin dynasty until the Ming, they withered and did not flourish;
the pond had long since become dry land. When the Master arrived at this mountain, white lotus flowers bloomed.
Contemporaries, remembering the ancient prophecy, all declared that the Master was the return of the Dharma Master Yuan. The Master [resided] from the Wuli era’s Yimao year until Geng...
He spent six years dwelling in the mountains, propagating the teachings of the Pure Land. Scholars from all directions came to join him, numbering no fewer than two thousand.
Later, at Jinling, he determined the time of his passing and passed away while sitting upright. Throughout his life, there were many miraculous occurrences, as detailed in his epitaph and biography.
His primary Dharma heir was Vinaya Master Jianyue.

The Vinaya Master’s posthumous name was Duti; his style name was Jianyue. His secular surname was Xu, and he was a native of Bailu Commandery in Southern Yunnan. His ancestral home was Jurong in Jiangnan.

At the beginning of the Hongwu era, when Yunnan and Qian were opened up, his grandfather was enfeoffed as General of the Righteous Martial (Zhao Wu Jiangjun) for his military merit and inherited the rank of Commander-in-Chief (Zhihui Shi).
Consequently, the family resided in Bailu for generations. His father was Yinchang, and his mother was Lady Wu. She dreamed of a bright moon falling [into her womb].
He was conceived with a natural affinity for the arts; from birth, he possessed a divine and quick intelligence. As he grew older, he displayed a vast talent and a liberated spirit.
He was skilled in painting, particularly excelling in portraits of the Great Being (Mahāsattva), which people vied to treasure. At that time, he was hailed as the "Little Wu Daozi.

When he was fourteen, both his parents passed away. His uncle, having no son, raised him as his heir. By the age of twenty-seven, he suddenly realized that the phenomena of the world are devoid of permanence.
Chang abandoned his inherited title and departed for Chidak Rock in Jianchuan Prefecture. There he met an elderly monk at a *ārāma* (monastery), with whom he shared a profound spiritual affinity.
The monk bestowed upon him the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; while reading the "World-Ruler’s Exquisite Adornment" chapter (*Lokadhātu-vyūha-parivarta*), he attained a deep realization.
He then went to Mount Baohong to seek ordination from Dharma Master Liangru. On the eve of this, Liangru dreamed of a person wearing a *kāṣāya*, surrounded and prostrated to by a multitude of monks.
He sought to receive the tonsure and ordination. When he saw his teacher at dawn, the teacher rejoiced, considering him a man of rebirth. He was subsequently granted the prohibitive precepts.
Having heard that there was Vinaya Master Samadhi in Jiangnan, he admired him; thus, accompanied by his friend Chengzhuo and carrying a gourd and a bamboo hat, he traveled eastward.
Enduring all manner of hardships, he first entered Mount Nanyue to visit the Wayman Duan, known as Sanduju Dao-ren, who was expounding the *Fourfold Reliance Commentary* on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Jidi ascended Mount Po'e and Mount Fengmao to pay homage at the various ancestral monasteries; he then proceeded to Mount Jiuhua and visited Mount Wutai.

Crossing the Great River once more, he finally met Master Mei at Haichao-an, where he received full ordination. He served as the *upādhyāya* (abbot) and took turns lecturing on the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*;
the fourfold assembly all praised him for his excellence. Yet the Master remained humble and felt he was not yet self-sufficient, so he searched through the Tripitaka for the four...
He examined the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā* and the monastic codes of other schools; wherever he encountered obstructions, he prayed to the Buddha for resolution.
After sitting in silent meditation for some time, his doubts were suddenly dispelled like melting ice. Subsequently, he received the full precepts from Master Mei at Ba’en Temple in Jinling.

Among the thousands of disciples in the assembly, as the Master was presiding over the ordination platform and instructing them, he suddenly recalled a past dream in which he had arrived at a great temple where gold and azure radiated with brilliance, and [there were] bhikṣus...

The assembly gathered like clouds. Looking upon himself, he already bore the appearance of a monk. A Gautama, clad in crimson robes, sat upon a high seat, inviting him to ascend and receive the scriptures, commanding him to preach.
The multitude all knelt to listen; he felt his sweat pouring down as he became aware of it. What he saw at that time was a vivid correspondence with his previous dream.

Later, he followed Master Mei to Mount Hua, where he served as a teacher while concurrently managing the affairs of the monastery. He neglected sleep and forgot to eat, remaining so from beginning to end.
Dai Mei. Master Mei once said to the assembly, "This old man’s banner of precepts for thirty years has nearly been broken, had it not been for the sight of the moon.
On the day he passed away, he took the Dharma robes of Princess Rongchang and various versions of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and entrusted them to him.
Upon succeeding to the seat, the Master exhorted the assembly with ten vows: first, not to ordain anyone as a disciple; second, not to accept funds for ordination.

Regarding the care of the elderly: (1) one shall not hoard bedding or provide sparse provisions; (2) one shall not accumulate incense or ritual implements; (3) one shall not privately prepare fruit or food;
(4) one shall not privately establish kitchens or storehouses; (5) one shall not avoid manual labor; (6) one shall not engage in visiting for condolences or congratulations;

(7) one shall not appoint a fundraising master to solicit donations; (8) silk garments and late meals are not permitted. Those who violate these agreements shall certainly not be allowed to remain. Hereafter—

He received full ordination according to the Vinaya and established boundaries for the summer retreat (*varṣā*). Those who saw or heard of him all said that it was as if the Master of the Southern Mountain had returned to this world.
In the third year of the Shunzhi era, government troops entered the mountains to search for local bandits; the Master and the entire assembly were all taken before the military headquarters.
At that time, Generals Ba and Ao were incensed by the Master’s dignified demeanor and intended to inflict the ultimate punishment upon him; all the temple’s permanent lands and properties—
He was imprisoned by the authorities. Although the Master was amidst a forest of swords and halberds, his countenance remained unchanged;

he replied with composure, "The main road to Mount Hua—how could it prevent people from coming and going? Consequently, the various officials of Ba and Qiao were moved to sincerity and respect, vowing to protect the Dharma.

They requested that the Master return to the mountain and restore the fields and lands, providing official documents for permanent reference. Thereupon, the Master personally practiced the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi*.
He entered samādhi and became a model for the assembly. For ninety days and nights, he neither sat nor lay down; he did this twice more.

Furthermore, following the legacy of Jetavana, he constructed a stone *śīla-maṇḍala* to the right of the Bronze Hall. On the night the foundation was excavated, he was moved by the manifestation of an auspicious omen from the Great Being (Mahāsattva), which appeared brilliantly.
The light from the maṇḍala and the hall intermingled, surging straight up to the Milky Way. When the Master opened the maṇḍala to recite the precepts, [the assembly] was small...
There were five thousand [monks] in attendance, reaching as many as fourteen thousand.
He accepted individual invitations at places such as Tianting in Changzhou, Wutai in Zhenzhou, Bifeng and Zilin in Jinling, Jile in Suqian, as well as his own mountain, Ciyun, and Tianlong.
Wherever he went, the streets were crowded with monastics and laypeople, old and young alike. When he was about to pass away, he manifested a slight illness.
He instructed his disciples, saying, "Do not administer medicinal broth; in seven days, my departure shall come. When the appointed time arrived, he sat upright and passed away.
The Master was born on the third day of the third month in the Xinchou year of the Wanli era. He entered parinirvāṇa on the twenty-second day of the first month in the Jiwu year of the Kangxi era.
His worldly age was seventy-nine, his monastic seniority forty-four, and he had spent three summer retreats in the mountains.
13. When the cremation took place seven days later, the fourfold assembly of disciples gathered from near and far.

Their lamentations filled the wilds, and the sound of their wailing shook the heavens. Within the radiant flames, some beheld the features of the Buddha; amidst the purple smoke, lotus flowers appeared.

After the fire was extinguished, his sacred remains were collected, and the five-colored *śarīra* relics obtained were beyond counting. Throughout the Master’s entire life, [he had performed] eight...
He sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). He conferred the precepts on more than seventy occasions.
There were over sixty dharma-heirs, and his disciples numbered in the tens of thousands. His writings include:
*Zhizhi huiji* (16 volumes), *Zuochi xushu* (15 volumes), *Chuanjie zhengfan* (4 volumes), *Dacheng xuanyi* (1 volume), *Yaoshi chanfa* (1 volume), *Tidu zhengfan* (1 volume), and *Sengxing guize*.

There are various texts, including the *One Scroll: The Correct Model for the Three Refuges and Five or Eight Precepts*, the *One Scroll: The Correct Model for Instructing Nuns*, the *One Scroll: The Black and White Poṣadha*, and the *One Scroll:
The Correct Model for the Mysterious and Dark Precepts*, all of which circulate in the world. His body was tall and large; his head possessed a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*);
his voice was like a great bell; and his appearance resembled that of an ancient Buddha. A virtuous man came from Duan-nan to pay his respects and said: "Your disciple has previously..."

He went to Mount Kukkutapāda to seek an audience with Mahākāśyapa. Moved by his sincerity, the deity Vaiśravaṇa appeared in a dream and informed him: "The Venerable One has already arrived at Mount Hua to propagate the Vinaya.

If you wish to behold him in person, you should go there. Thus, he came to pay his respects. Fearing that the assembly might be confused, the Master kept this secret and did not allow it to be transmitted.
Consequently, the dried-up spring at Malin-gorge overflowed on its own, and the three generations of grievances at Longmian were extinguished—these were the results of his hidden instructions.
I take refuge. The divine dragons who protect the Dharma and their various miraculous manifestations are too numerous to record in full.

For further details, one should consult the two inscriptions for the pagodas of Supervising Intendant Li Mo and Duhe Sun Zaifeng, as well as the biographies of the Hanlin Academician You Tong and Attendant Censor Fang Xiangxian, and the stele inscription for the conduct of Provincial Governor Ding Sikong.
There was a Vinaya Master named Yijie, a dharma heir of our teacher. His name was Shuyu; "Yijie" is his courtesy name, and his pen-name is Fo'an.
He currently resides at Zhaokong Temple in ancient Hangzhou, preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. His scholarly talent is preeminent and his virtue is lofty and brilliant;
he is truly a hero of this age, one who does not disgrace himself as the fourth-generation descendant of the venerable patriarch Huiyun.
In the summer of the *xin-si* year, I accepted an invitation and traveled to Kōmura Castle in Higo Province, where I lectured on the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* at Shingo Kyōji Temple.
Subsequently, the abbot of Kōtō Zenji Temple in Karatsu Castle, Hizen Province, earnestly requested that I open the precept ordination ceremony at his temple;
consequently, I remained there to observe the winter *anagya*. Before the conclusion of the retreat, the abbot of the former temple requested that I visit Nagasaki. Upon my arrival there, first—
I visited Xingfu Temple on Mount Dongming. The abbot, Chan Master Yuefeng Zhang, is a native of China.
He rejoiced at my visit and treated me with generous hospitality. We sat together upon mats and conversed; his words flowed forth like falling jade dust.
He presented me with a gift of two fascicles of the *Pini riyong qieyao xiangru ji* (The Essential Incense-Milk Record of Daily Use in the Vinaya), which is the same as the *Jianyue*.
Furthermore, there was that which had been collected; the Vinaya Master Jie then annotated it accordingly, titling it the *Xiangru ji* (Record of Fragrant Milk).
I respectfully read it and, through what the Zen Master discussed, learned for the first time that the Vinaya Master was currently at Zhaoqing Temple.

Thereupon, I entrusted the Zen Master with a diagram of the six requisites (*ṣaḍ-vastu*) and a copy of the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* in four fascicles, sending them by merchant ship as a gift. Upon seeing them, the Vinaya Master rejoiced and composed a preface.
I have verified this and received from him the two fascicles of his own work, the *Karmavācanā-vidhi* (羯磨儀式), which he presented to me.
On the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month of this year, the Wuzi year, I respectfully accepted them. I have composed a verse to record my joy.
My previous gift was based on the *Śāstra*, while this present gift I have received relies upon the diligent efforts of Master Dongming. Since the preface has already been printed, [I record this].
Placed at the beginning of this volume, I privately fear that people may not discern its origins; therefore, I have composed a "Record of the Origins" (*yuanqi*).
All the facts concerning the various masters are drawn from the *Xiangru ji* (Record of Incense and Milk), supplemented by the *Lushan zhi* (Annals of Mount Lu).

I have preserved the texts in their entirety and dared not abridge them, so that people may know that within the Chinese tradition of the Vinaya, there has been one who successfully inherited and restored it, thereby preserving the Buddha’s [teachings].
It is said that the Way’s life-span endures through this age of turbid decline.
Written on the third day after the winter solstice in the year of Tuwei Kundun, the fifth year of the Bōei era.
Discourse on the Bhikṣu Zhantang Shupan of the An-yang Aranya in Jiangzuo, by Tan Shi.
